E048-01.notes: 'was sitting on a Florida beach when he had an idea' needs no punctuation; 'when he had an idea' is a dependent clause tied to the main clause. A puts a comma between the subordinator 'when' and its clause. C uses a semicolon before a dependent clause, so it leaves a fragment. D puts a comma between the subject 'he' and the verb 'had'.

E048-02.notes: 'just as dots and dashes stood for letters' sets up a precise parallel comparison. B 'just like how' is wordy and informal. C 'the same as when' wrongly makes it about time. D 'as if' wrongly suggests something hypothetical or contrary to fact.

E048-03.notes: The two clauses contrast: they got a patent, yet the equipment cost too much. B 'so' and D 'and as a result' make the expensive equipment a result of the patent, which is illogical. C 'because' makes it the cause of the patent, also illogical.

flags.note: Once sentence 7 moves before sentence 6, 'Their version' follows sentence 5, where the only plural nouns are 'Wide and narrow lines' and 'dots and dashes'. The intended antecedent (Woodland and Silver) is two sentences back, in sentence 2. Students can still work it out, but the pronoun reads loosely. Something like 'The pair's version' would read more cleanly.

E048-04.notes: Sentence 7 describes the design: circles, read from any direction. It belongs right after the idea forms (sentence 5) and before the patent for 'their design' (sentence 6). That also keeps sentence 6, where the equipment is too expensive, next to sentence 8, where the idea sits unused. A leaves 7 interrupting the cost-to-unused-idea link. B puts the design description after the two-decade gap, which is out of order. D drops it into the 1974 paragraph, where it does not fit.

E048-05.notes: Both sides are independent clauses, so a semicolon works. A is a comma splice. C is a fused sentence, and it misreads as 'unused grocers'. D 'and so because' is redundant and ungrammatical.

E048-06.notes: The previous paragraph ends with the idea unused because scanning was impractical. C answers that with 'however' and cheap lasers and chips, which leads into the 1974 scan. A is an irrelevant aside about other uses of lasers. B is a technical detail with no link to the previous paragraph. D goes back over the past and does not lead into the first scan.

E048-07.notes: The plural subject 'barcodes' takes 'are', and 'Today' calls for present tense. A, C and D are singular, and D is also past tense.

E048-08.notes: The essay traces the barcode from the beach sketch to the patent, the stalled years, the 1974 scan and wide use today. A is false: the essay never explains how lasers read barcodes. B is false: the friendship is only mentioned. C is false: the essay gives the date and place (June 26, 1974, Troy, Ohio).

E048-09.notes: The detail about the lighthouse's geography breaks up the paragraph about the lens's effect (installation, then 'The improvement was dramatic'). A is wrong because the sentence gives no reason Cordouan was chosen. C is wrong because location says nothing about visibility range. D is wrong because the sentence agrees with 'in France'; it does not contradict it.

E048-10.notes: Sentence 10 gives a concrete example of the 'dramatic' improvement, going from a few miles to more than twenty. A 'However' and B 'Nevertheless' signal contrast, but there is none. D 'Instead' signals replacement, which does not fit.

E048-11.notes: The plural subject 'lenses' needs a plural verb. A past narrative ('Within a few decades' of 1823) calls for 'had been installed'. A 'has been' and C 'was' are singular, so they disagree with 'lenses'. D 'had installed' is active, which wrongly makes the lenses the ones doing the installing.

E048-12.notes: The essay shows how Fresnel's study of how light bends produced a lighter, more effective lens that replaced wasteful mirrors. A is false: no list of lighthouses is given. C is false: the keepers appear in only one clause. D is false: sentence 6 explains how the prisms bent light into a horizontal beam.

E048-13.notes: The phrase gives the brand name, Craft Master, which appears nowhere else in the essay. A is wrong because the phrase does not explain why sales rose; sentence 6 does that. C is wrong because the name has not been given before. D is wrong because a brand name contradicts nothing.
